title: Praise at Age One, Mindset at Seven
text:
Earlier laboratory studies by Carol Dweck and others suggested that the way adults praise children affects how they think about ability. Elizabeth Gunderson, Susan Levine and their colleagues at the University of Chicago wanted to know whether ordinary praise in everyday family life had lasting effects.

They visited the homes of 53 families in the Chicago area and filmed parents and their children going about normal activities for ninety minutes, when the children were about fourteen months old, then again at about twenty-six and thirty-eight months. The researchers coded every instance of praise. Process praise focused on effort or actions, such as "you worked hard" or "good throwing." Person praise focused on fixed qualities, such as "you're so smart" or "good girl."

Five years later, when the children were seven and eight, the team measured their attitudes: whether they preferred challenging tasks, and whether they believed that abilities like intelligence could be improved with effort.

The more of parents' praise had been process praise in those toddler years, the more the children later favored challenge and believed ability can grow. Boys had received more process praise than girls, and boys were correspondingly more likely to have these attitudes. Total praise and person praise did not predict the outcome in the same way.
lesson: Even with toddlers, praise what they do, how they try and what strategy they use. Those everyday words shape how a child will face challenges years later.
people: Elizabeth Gunderson, Sarah Gripshover, Carissa Romero, Carol Dweck, Susan Goldin-Meadow, Susan Levine
source: Gunderson, E. A., Gripshover, S. J., Romero, C., Dweck, C. S., Goldin-Meadow, S., and Levine, S. C. (2013). Parent praise to 1- to 3-year-olds predicts children's motivational frameworks 5 years later. Child Development, 84(5), 1526-1541.
caveat: The sample was small and the findings correlational, so other features of the families may explain part of the link.
